newsitem.title: USA: State Farm to take over 100,000 Florida policies.
newsitem.headline: State Farm to take over 100,000 Florida policies.

text.p: State Farm Insurance Cos. agreed Thursday to provide homeowners insurance coverage to an additional 100,000 homes in Florida, where it has frozen the issuance of new policies for the past five years.

The state's largest insurer, State Farm stopped writing new policies after Hurricane Andrew ripped through South Florida Aug. 24, 1992. Since then, state insurance officials have been urging the company to get back into Florida markets and relieve pressure on the state.
Under the plan announced Thursday, State Farm agreed to offer coverage to homeowners outside the state's most hurricane prone counties in south Florida and around Tampa Bay.
The agreement comes six weeks after an arbitration board voted to allow the company to increase rates by an average of 24 percent statewide.

In agreeing to take on additional customers, State Farm joins AllState Insurance Co., which pledged in July to take an additional 127,000 clients, many of whom are now insured by a state-sponsored underwriting association.

"I am please to advise you, that, due to a combination of exposure reducing activities and rate adjustments now in place, State Farm is in a position to take on some additional policy holders," said State Farm Vice President Kim Brunner in a letter to Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson.

Nelson and insurers have been wrangling for the past few years over the availability of homeowners insurance in the wake of Andrew, which caused nearly $16 billion in claims when it hit South Florida in 1992.
Since that time, many private insurers have stopped issuing new policies and a state-run insurance pool, the Joint Underwriting Association, now counts more than 700,000 policy holders.
Nelson lost out last month when a newly created arbitration board overruled his rejection of State Farm's rate hike.
The commissioner, however, said the company's pledge to take in new policyholders by the end of 1998 was the second welcomed response from State Farm in less than a month.
In July, the company agreed not to seek another rate hike until 1999.

"This is another step in restoring competition among homeowner insurers in most areas of the state," Nelson said. "But, as State Farm's response demonstrates, there is still a shortfall of affordable insurance for homeowners in South Florida and the Tampa Bay area."
